items.title: Frank Chace Interview, 1961-11-18
items.q: Vali spoke of playing with Keppard.

ctx.x: I know Vali's early work mainly from a record, I think 1924, under Spaniard's name. Why can't it be Poor Little Me and Everybody Loves My Baby? And... Gee, it's hard. I don't know where to place Vali. Vali, all I know is that I thought that was a wonderful record. Vali played beautifully. Now this is, of course, before Tesh, before Pee Wee. Where he got it from, who knows, John?

Well, I have a suggestion. Vali spoke of playing with Keppard. It probably was at Lorraine Gardens, and probably they allowed him to play the first set or two until Buster Bailey came over. He was playing on a theater job, I believe, and then played with Keppard later in the evening. But Vali was allowed to sit in until Vali came over. Now this sounds, if this is true, and was two or three years earlier, sounds as if both Buster Bailey and Vali might have been influenced by what was happening on the south side.…

Well, that makes us suppose that Vali had no white influences at all at that time. He was listening strictly to the colored bands. And, of course, the great question under discussion is where did the distinctively hot style come from that we identify with the Chicago white clarinet players? It must be something innate. They were nervous or something? Who knows? They were desperate or anxious or something, and they got this particular quality into their playing that the colored players didn't have. Who knows?…
